result.summary: Penelope fetches Ulysses' bow and proposes a contest of stringing it and shooting through twelve axes. The suitors and Telemachus fail, Ulysses reveals himself to Eumaeus and Philoetius, and the beggar is given the bow. He strings it and shoots through the axes, and Telemachus arms himself beside him.

scenes.title: Penelope fetches the bow
scenes.summary: Minerva inspires Penelope, who opens the store-room and takes down Ulysses' bow. Its origin is told: Iphitus gave it to Ulysses in Messene.
scenes.stakes: Penelope's household and her own future depend on the contest she begins.

scenes.title: Penelope proposes the contest
scenes.summary: Penelope brings the bow to the suitors and promises to marry whoever strings it and shoots through twelve axes. Antinous scolds the weeping servants.
scenes.stakes: Penelope must leave her house with a new husband if a suitor wins.

scenes.title: Telemachus and suitors fail
scenes.summary: Telemachus sets up the axes and almost strings the bow before Ulysses checks him. Leiodes and the other suitors fail even after warming and greasing it.
scenes.stakes: The suitors risk disgrace; Telemachus tries to keep his mother in the house.

scenes.title: Ulysses reveals himself
scenes.summary: Outside, Ulysses tests Eumaeus and Philoetius, then shows his scar and gives instructions for the coming fight.
scenes.stakes: If the two servants betray him, the plan to destroy the suitors fails.

place.name: the outer yard of Ulysses' house

scenes.title: The beggar asks for the bow
scenes.summary: Eurymachus fails and Antinous postpones the contest. Ulysses asks to try the bow; Antinous threatens him, Penelope defends him, and Telemachus sends her upstairs.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses risks exposure and violence from the suitors.

scenes.title: Ulysses strings the bow
scenes.summary: Telemachus forces Eumaeus to deliver the bow. The doors are secured, and Ulysses strings it and shoots through the axes. He signals Telemachus, who arms himself.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses must succeed in his first move against the suitors while outnumbered.

notable_quotes.reason: Ulysses reveals himself after twenty years.
The decisive shot through the twelve axes.
Vivid simile of the bowstring singing like a swallow.

analysis.text: The bow contest tests identity and legitimacy: only the true king can string it, while the suitors' failure exposes them.
Guest-friendship (xenia) is central; Hercules' murder of his guest Iphitus is condemned, and the suitors' abuse of a beggar breaks the same norm.

legacy.text: The bow of Ulysses became a lasting symbol of a test only the rightful person can pass, echoed in many later tales.

fun_facts.text: Exactly how the arrow passes through twelve axes has long puzzled scholars, who debate whether the axe heads had rings or holes.

language_notes.text: This is a section heading summarizing the book's events, not part of the narrative itself.
Lacedaemon is the region of Sparta in the southern Peloponnese; the translation places the meeting there, though the scene itself is set in Messene.
"A debt owing from the whole people" means compensation demanded from Messene collectively for the stolen sheep, not from one individual.
"Feared not heaven's vengeance, nor respected his own table" means Hercules broke the sacred duty of hospitality, which the gods were thought to punish.
"Loosed the strap": the door was fastened by a thong looped round the handle, which she undid before using the key to push back the bolts.
The "cloister" here means the colonnaded hall or porch of the house where the suitors sit, not a monastery.
"Bearing-posts" are the pillars that hold up the roof of the hall.
"Whomsoever of you shall string it most easily" means whoever strings it with the least effort. Stringing the bow needed great strength.
Penelope says she will remember this house even in her dreams, meaning she will never forget it after leaving.
"Stockman" is Philoetius, the herdsman who looks after Ulysses' cattle. "Hard by" means close by.
"Such another as Ulysses" means anyone equal to Ulysses.
"Jove must have robbed me of my senses": Telemachus is pretending to be foolish, attributing his lighthearted behavior to divine interference, as Greeks often did.
Pylos, Argos and Mycene are major Greek cities of the Peloponnese; Ithaca is Ulysses' island. Together they cover the whole known world of suitors' origins.
"Made straight by line": the groove was aligned with a taut cord, as a carpenter would, so the axe holes line up for the shot.
The bracketed words are the translator's clarification of which door is meant.
Going to the right means proceeding left to right around the hall, the customary direction for passing wine.
"Lard": animal fat. Greasing and warming the bow was meant to make the dry horn and wood more supple.
Cloisters here means the covered colonnades around the courtyard of Ulysses' house, not a monastery.
"What manner of men would you be" means what kind of men would you show yourselves to be, how loyal.
"With might and main" is an idiom meaning with all one's strength.
The scar comes from a boar hunt in Ulysses' youth; it is the same mark by which his nurse Eurycleia recognised him earlier.
"The sun would have gone down upon their mourning" means they would have wept until nightfall.
"Token" means a prearranged signal for the action to begin.
A festival day of Apollo, god of archery, when stringing a bow was supposedly improper or ill-omened; Antinous uses this as a face-saving excuse.
Mixing-bowls: wine was mixed with water in large bowls before serving; 'drink-offering' means a libation poured to the gods before drinking.
Antinous alludes to the myth of the drunken Centaur Eurytion, who disrupted the wedding of Peirithous, king of the Lapithae, and was mutilated.
Echetus is a legendary cruel king who mutilates and kills visitors; the name is used here as a threat.
'Over against Elis' means the islands lying off the coast of Elis in the western Peloponnese, a way of naming the whole region.
Distaff: a staff that holds wool or flax for spinning.
The suitor's curse: Eumaeus's own hounds, the boarhounds he keeps, would tear him apart in some secluded spot. It is a grim joke on his role as swineherd.
Byblus fibre is papyrus, used for making ropes. The cable is a ship's rope repurposed to bar the gates.
A peg is the tuning peg of a lyre; the twisted gut is the string, so stringing a lyre is the comparison for stringing the bow.
Saturn (the Greek Cronus) is the father of Jove (Zeus). The thunder is taken as Jove's sign approving Ulysses' act.
The arrows 'the Achaeans were about to taste' is a grim euphemism: the other arrows in the quiver will be used to kill the suitors.
The axes were set in a row, and the arrow had to pass through the holes in their handles, or helve-sockets, in one straight shot.
Ulysses speaks ambiguously: 'prepare supper' secretly means the suitors' deaths are coming, while he appears to suggest only a normal banquet.
The eyebrow sign is the prearranged signal to Telemachus to arm himself and join his father in the fight.

context_notes.text: Minerva (the Greek Athena) is Ulysses' divine protector. Her prompting sets the contest that leads to the suitors' deaths.
Hercules, son of Jove, was famed for his great labours and strength, but also for violent fits of temper.
Leaving the bow at home meant it was preserved, ready to serve as the instrument of Ulysses' return.
The iron and bronze were prizes Ulysses had won, and they were stored in the treasure room with the bow.
The twelve axes are set in a row. The archer must shoot an arrow cleanly through all their holes, a feat only Ulysses was known to manage.
Ulysses, still disguised as a beggar, secretly signals his son to stop, since he wants himself to be the one to string the bow.
Leiodes serves as the suitors' sacrificial priest and diviner, a religious role that sets him apart from the rest.
Antinous and Eurymachus are the leading suitors, so their failure will be the decisive one.
Ulysses is still disguised as a beggar. He has been testing the household while planning the slaughter of the suitors.
Autolycus was Ulysses' maternal grandfather, a famous trickster and thief. Ulysses visited him on Mt. Parnassus as a youth.
The bow is the contest the suitors have been attempting, and Ulysses needs it in hand to begin his revenge.
Thigh bones wrapped in fat were burned as the god's share in a sacrifice; Apollo is the archer god.
Ulysses is disguised as a beggar, so he must ask for the bow without revealing himself.
Telemachus asserts that women's duties are domestic, using this convention to get Penelope out of the hall before the crucial moment.
Telemachus asserts his authority as master of the house, though he is young. The suitors do not yet know he is aiding the beggar.
Euryclea is the old nurse of the household. Locking the women in keeps them safe and prevents anyone from raising an alarm.
Philoetius is the loyal cowherd. He secures the gates so no suitor can escape or call for help.

literary_notes.text: The mention of the suitors' "destruction" announces the coming slaughter, turning a seemingly harmless contest into a deadly trap.
The story of Iphitus's murder interrupts the action, giving the bow a history of friendship and violated hospitality.
The doors flying open "like a bull bellowing in a meadow" compares the loud creak of the bolts to an animal's roar.
Penelope's bitter weeping before she acts shows her grief and the pain of the choice she is making.
Antinous admits no suitor equals Ulysses yet mocks the servants' grief. He does not know that Ulysses is standing among them.
The narrator tells us Antinous will be the first to die by Ulysses' arrows, while he and the suitors still feel confident.
The suitors see only a beggar's gesture; the reader knows Ulysses is secretly directing his son and preparing his own turn.
Telemachus plays the weak, uncertain youth, covering for his father's signal while showing his obedient cunning.
Leiodes' words that the bow will take the life of many a chief unknowingly predict the coming slaughter.
Antinous mocks the idea that the bow could kill chiefs, though it will soon kill him.
Ulysses poses a hypothetical about his own return, while the servants do not know he stands before them.
"I have suffered much" compresses twenty years of war, wandering and loss into a plain phrase.
Recognition by the scar recurs in the poem as proof of identity, and here it prompts tears and embraces.
'Craftily' reminds us of Ulysses' cunning: his polite, pious request hides his true purpose.
Antinous cites myth as a warning, though ironically he himself resembles the unruly guest who abuses a host's house.
Eurymachus imagines a beggar stringing the bow as a shameful fantasy, but the audience knows it is about to happen.
Penelope's sleep, sent by Minerva, removes her from the hall before the coming slaughter.
The suitors guess he is a bow-fancier, while the reader knows he is the bow's owner and their coming destroyer.
Ulysses' ease with the bow is likened to a bard fitting a lyre string, linking music and archery and showing his mastery.
The bowstring's sound is compared to a swallow's twittering, a gentle image that contrasts with the deadly purpose of the shot.
Jove's thunder and the suitors' dismay signal divine support for Ulysses and the coming slaughter.
